claims.claim: in theory the smallest prey a cannibal can take decides between regulation and single-cohort cycles (Claessen et al. 2002)
claims.location: p. 1660 (PDF p. 1), Abstract; pp. 1666–1667 (PDF pp. 7–8), effects of δ; p. 1673 (PDF p. 14), Discussion
claims.quote: With low δ, cannibalism regulates recruitment, resulting in coexistence of many year classes.
claims.conditions: a physiologically structured model of one cannibalistic fish population (parameterized for Eurasian perch) with one shared zooplankton resource (Daphnia); δ is the LOWER LIMIT OF THE PREY:CANNIBAL LENGTH RATIO (the 'predation window'), not an absolute prey size
claims.note: The abstract: for large δ cannibalism cannot decimate young-of-year cohorts and size-dependent competition gives recruit-driven single-cohort cycles; low δ gives regulation by cannibalism; intermediate δ alternates the two (with dwarfs and giants). Strictly it is the smallest prey RELATIVE to the cannibal's length (δ = 0.06 for Eurasian perch). The Discussion links this to the sentence's other half: Crystal Lake yellow perch (Sanderson et al. 1999) show cohort dominance resembling single-cohort cycles, which the authors attribute to yellow perch's narrower predation window (higher δ) than Eurasian perch's.

notes: A crude rule of thumb is given (p. 1673): cannibalism may regulate a population only if δ is smaller than (or close to) the ratio of length at birth (or first feeding) to length at maturation. Upper limit ε governs stunting vs giants, not the dynamics.
